subject.original: Paw protection on rock and scree. Check your dog's paws during the walk and consider boots on rough terrain.

result.title: Editorial proposal: Paw protection on rock and scree
result.summary: The proposal makes two targeted changes: a clearer paw-check routine and observable turn-back cues. It does not change the guide structure or imply that every dog needs boots.

changes.before: Check your dog's paws during the walk and consider boots on rough terrain.
changes.after: Check your dog’s pads before the walk, again at the first rest, and after sustained rock or scree. Boots can help some dogs on abrasive ground, but poor fit may cause rubbing. Test them on a short walk before relying on them in the mountains.
changes.reason: Adds an actionable inspection rhythm and preserves the caveat that boots are not automatically beneficial.

changes.before: Turn back if your dog is uncomfortable.
changes.after: Stop and inspect the paw if your dog begins licking a foot, shortening a stride, hesitating on familiar ground, or repeatedly shifting weight. Turn back if the change persists.
changes.reason: Replaces a vague instruction with observable behaviour without diagnosing an injury.

sources.label: American Veterinary Medical Association, pet care
sources.supports: General preventive care and escalation to veterinary care when injury is suspected.

openQuestions: Should ORMA require veterinary review before publishing specific injury signs?
